fuehrerschein-vorfahrt.title: Priority, turning and pedestrians: reading a scenario
fuehrerschein-vorfahrt.description: The first course unit for the driving-licence module. Two lessons work through six labelled junction diagrams - from plain right-before-left with two cars to a four-party case (car from the left, cyclist, pedestrian) - deriving the correct answer from the text of the StVO in each case, section by section and sentence by sentence. A third lesson is background on the examination format: since 1 April 2014 the theory test has also included tasks built on film sequences. All diagrams are original schematic drawings. Note: unofficial practice material, not legally reviewed, and no substitute for training at a driving school.

fs-u1.title: Six junction scenarios, derived from the regulation

fs-u2.title: Exam format: video questions (background, not quizzed)

fs-l1.title: Right-before-left - and when that is not the question

fs-l1-s1.title: Four questions, always in this order
fs-l1-s1.body:
To answer "who goes first?" at a junction, work through a fixed order of questions. It falls straight out of the way the StVO is structured. (Statutory quotations below are translations of the German original; the German text is what governs.)

1. Is there a special rule in force? § 8(1) sentence 1 StVO: "At crossroads and junctions, whoever comes from the right has priority." Sentence 2 carves out exactly two cases - "where priority is specially regulated by traffic signs (signs 205, 206, 301, 306)" and "for vehicles entering another road from a field or forest track". Traffic lights and a police officer's signals override all of this in any case: § 37(1) sentence 1 StVO - "Light signals take precedence over priority rules and over traffic signs regulating priority" - and § 36(1) StVO - "The signals and instructions of police officers are to be obeyed. They take precedence over all other orders and other rules, but do not release the road user from their duty of care." If none of those apply, right-before-left applies, with no further exceptions.

2. Is anyone turning? Priority and turning are two separate sets of rules. § 8 settles who may enter the junction. § 9 additionally governs whom a turning vehicle must let through - even where that vehicle itself has priority.

3. Is a bicycle involved? A bicycle is a vehicle. § 2(1) sentence 1 StVO: "Vehicles must use the carriageways; where there are two carriageways, the right-hand one." Someone cycling on the carriageway is therefore ordinary vehicle traffic, and right-before-left applies to them exactly as it does to a car. § 9(3) also names bicycles expressly.

4. Is anyone on foot? This is where the most common misconception sits. "Pedestrians always have priority" appears nowhere in the StVO. There are two different provisions - § 26 for pedestrian crossings (zebra crossings) and § 25(3) for crossing the carriageway anywhere else - plus § 9(3) sentence 3 when a vehicle is turning. Which one applies depends on where the person crosses and on what the vehicle is doing.

Above all of it sits § 1 StVO. Paragraph 1: "Participation in road traffic requires constant caution and mutual consideration." Paragraph 2: "Anyone taking part in traffic must behave in such a way that no other person is harmed, endangered, or obstructed or inconvenienced more than is unavoidable in the circumstances." Having priority and still having to brake is not a contradiction - it is the normal case.

About the drawings on the following pages: the blue vehicle with the white roof dot is always you. The letters A, B, C, D only identify the road users - they are not an order of precedence. Arrows show where someone intends to go. The diagrams are deliberately schematic: they show geometry and intent, not one particular real junction.

fs-l1-s2.title: Scenario 1: unsigned crossroads, two cars
fs-l1-s2.body:
A crossroads inside a built-up area. No priority signs, no traffic lights, no police officer; both roads are ordinary roads, not a field or forest track. A (you) approach from the bottom, going straight on. B comes from the right, also going straight on.

Who goes first? B.

§ 8(1) sentence 1 StVO: "At crossroads and junctions, whoever comes from the right has priority." From your point of view, B is on your right. Sentence 2 allows only two exceptions - regulation by signs 205, 206, 301 or 306, and vehicles coming from a field or forest track. Neither is present here, so right-before-left applies unchanged.

Your duty to wait has to be visible early, not only at the stopping point. § 8(2) sentence 1 StVO: "Anyone who has to observe priority must show in good time through their driving behaviour, in particular through moderate speed, that they are waiting." Under sentence 2 you may only proceed "if it can be seen that whoever has priority will be neither endangered nor substantially obstructed". Where the location has poor visibility, sentence 3 permits you to "edge cautiously into the crossroads or junction until visibility is given".

Order: B, then A.
fs-l1-s2.alt_text: Schematic top-down view of a crossroads with no traffic signs and no markings. Vehicle A - blue, with a white roof dot, your car - approaches from the bottom; an arrow points straight ahead, upwards. Vehicle B - dark grey - approaches from the right; an arrow points straight ahead, to the left. No signs, no traffic light, no road markings other than the centre lines.
fs-l1-s2.caption: Unsigned crossroads: right-before-left under § 8(1) sentence 1 StVO.

fs-l1-s3.title: Scenario 2: the vehicle from the right is a cyclist
fs-l1-s3.body:
The same unsigned crossroads. This time the road user coming from the right is not a car but a cyclist - riding on the carriageway; there is no cycle track. A (you) intend to go straight on.

Who goes first? The cyclist.

§ 8(1) sentence 2 StVO lists exactly two exceptions to right-before-left: signs 205, 206, 301, 306 - and vehicles entering another road from a field or forest track. "Bicycle" does not appear in that list. A bicycle is a vehicle; § 2(1) sentence 1 StVO: "Vehicles must use the carriageways; where there are two carriageways, the right-hand one." A cyclist on the carriageway is therefore ordinary vehicle traffic, and right-before-left applies to them as it does to a car.

The common counter-assumption - "slower, therefore must yield", or "bikes always have to wait" - has no basis in the regulation. § 8(2) sentence 2 StVO only lets you proceed "if it can be seen that whoever has priority will be neither endangered nor substantially obstructed". A cyclist is easier to overlook than a car - not less entitled.

Order: B, then A.
fs-l1-s3.alt_text: Schematic top-down view of the same unsigned crossroads. Vehicle A - blue, with a white roof dot, your car - approaches from the bottom, arrow pointing straight ahead. From the right comes B, a cyclist shown as a dark blue bicycle pictogram with an arrow pointing left; the cyclist is on the carriageway and no cycle track is drawn.
fs-l1-s3.caption: A bicycle on the carriageway is vehicle traffic - § 2(1) sentence 1 StVO. Right-before-left applies unchanged.

fs-l1-s4.title: Scenario 3: you turn right, the cyclist goes straight on
fs-l1-s4.body:
Here the priority question is not the point at all. A (you) intend to turn right. A cycle track runs alongside your carriageway on the right, and B is continuing straight on along it in your direction of travel. Your turning path crosses the cycle track.

Who goes first? B.

§ 9(3) sentence 1 StVO: "Anyone intending to turn must let oncoming vehicles through, and must also let rail vehicles, mopeds, bicycles and light electric vehicles through where they are travelling on or alongside the carriageway in the same direction." That is exactly this case: same direction, alongside the carriageway. You must let B through.

This is not a priority rule. Priority under § 8 decides who may enter the junction; § 9(3) applies in addition and independently of it. Even on a priority road you may not cut across straight-ahead cycle traffic when turning.

For heavy vehicles there is a further provision. § 9(6) StVO: "Anyone driving a motor vehicle with a permissible gross mass over 3.5 t within a built-up area must drive at walking pace when turning right, where straight-ahead cycle traffic on or alongside the carriageway, or pedestrian traffic crossing the carriageway in the immediate area of the turn, is to be expected." That walking-pace duty does not apply to a class B car - the duty to let cyclists through under paragraph 3 applies regardless.

Order: B, then A.
fs-l1-s4.alt_text: Schematic top-down view of a junction. Vehicle A - blue, with a white roof dot, your car - approaches from the bottom; a curved arrow shows its right-turn path. A red-brown cycle track runs alongside the carriageway on the right and continues across the junction. On that track, B - a bicycle pictogram with a straight arrow pointing up - carries on in the same direction as A. A's turning arrow crosses the cycle track.
fs-l1-s4.caption: Turning is not a priority case: § 9(3) sentence 1 StVO names bicycles expressly.

fs-l2.title: People on foot, zebra crossings, and the four-party case

fs-l2-s1.title: Scenario 4: a pedestrian, and no zebra crossing
fs-l2-s1.body:
An open stretch of road inside a built-up area: no junction, no markings, no pedestrian crossing, no traffic lights. A (you) are driving straight on. B steps off the kerb between two parked cars, intending to cross.

Who has priority? You do - not B.

This is where the everyday rule "pedestrians always have priority" is demonstrably wrong. § 26(1) sentence 1 StVO ties pedestrian priority expressly to a pedestrian crossing: "At pedestrian crossings, vehicles other than rail vehicles must enable persons on foot ... to cross the carriageway." There is no pedestrian crossing here, so § 26 does not apply at all.

What does apply is § 25(3) StVO, and it puts the duty on B. Sentence 1: "A person on foot must cross carriageways briskly, by the shortest route, at right angles to the direction of travel, having regard to vehicular traffic." Sentence 2 goes further: where traffic density, vehicle speed, visibility or the flow of traffic require it, a carriageway is to be crossed "only at crossroads or junctions, at traffic lights within markings, at pedestrian crossing aids, or at pedestrian crossings (sign 293)".

And this is precisely where it does not stop. Having priority does not mean being allowed to drive on. § 1(2) StVO: "Anyone taking part in traffic must behave in such a way that no other person is harmed, endangered, or obstructed or inconvenienced more than is unavoidable in the circumstances." If B is already on the carriageway you must brake - not because B has priority, but because § 1(2), and the "constant caution and mutual consideration" of § 1(1), require it. Between parked cars, people stepping out is to be expected anyway; the right response here is not to assert priority but to come off the accelerator.

Worth memorising: B is in the wrong and you still have to stop. Both at once, with no contradiction.
fs-l2-s1.alt_text: Schematic top-down view of a straight road with footway strips on both sides, no junction, and no road markings other than the centre line. Vehicle A - blue, with a white roof dot, your car - travels from left to right with an arrow in its direction of travel. Further right, two light grey cars are parked at the kerb. Between them, B - a pedestrian pictogram - steps onto the carriageway; an arrow points across the road, upwards. No zebra crossing and no traffic light are drawn.
fs-l2-s1.caption: With no pedestrian crossing, § 25(3) StVO applies, not § 26 - but § 1(2) StVO always applies.

fs-l2-s2.title: Scenario 5: a zebra crossing - with a cyclist riding across it
fs-l2-s2.body:
The same road, but now with a marked pedestrian crossing - sign 293, the broad white bars across the carriageway. A (you) are approaching it. B is standing at the kerb and clearly intends to cross. C is riding a bicycle onto the markings from the other side.

For B the answer is clear: you must enable B to cross. § 26(1) sentence 1 StVO: "At pedestrian crossings, vehicles other than rail vehicles must enable persons on foot, and users of invalid carriages or wheelchairs, who are evidently intending to use the crossing, to cross the carriageway." Sentence 2: "They may then approach only at moderate speed; if necessary, they must wait." Two further duties come with it: "Overtaking is prohibited at crossings" (paragraph 3), and where traffic is stop-and-go you may not drive onto the crossing if you would have to wait on it (paragraph 2).

For C the answer is different, and this surprises many people. The list in § 26(1) sentence 1 reads: persons on foot, and users of invalid carriages or wheelchairs. Cyclists are not in it. Someone riding across the zebra crossing therefore gains no priority from § 26. If that same person dismounts and pushes the bike, they are a person on foot - § 25(2) StVO speaks expressly of persons on foot "who are bringing vehicles with them" - and are then covered by paragraph 1.

Paragraph 4 governs the converse case: "Where the marking leads across a cycle track or another part of the road, these provisions apply accordingly." That gives cycle traffic no priority; it obliges cyclists too to let people on foot cross where the marking is carried over the cycle track.

Having no priority is still not permission to drive at C. § 1(2) StVO applies here as it did in scenario 4. In practice: let B through because § 26(1) requires it; let C through because a collision has to be avoided either way.

Order: B (and, in practice, C too), then A.
fs-l2-s2.alt_text: Schematic top-down view of a straight road with footway strips. Five broad white bars lie across the carriageway - a pedestrian crossing, sign 293. Vehicle A - blue, with a white roof dot, your car - approaches the crossing from the left. B, a pedestrian pictogram, stands at the lower kerb at the markings; an arrow points across the road, upwards. C, a bicycle pictogram, rides onto the markings from above; an arrow points downwards. No upright sign is depicted, only the marking itself.
fs-l2-s2.caption: § 26(1) sentence 1 StVO names persons on foot and users of invalid carriages or wheelchairs - not cyclists who stay in the saddle.

fs-l2-s3.title: Scenario 6: a car from the left, a cyclist, a pedestrian - four road users
fs-l2-s3.body:
The composite case, and the only one in this course with four road users. An unsigned crossroads. A (you) approach from the bottom and intend to turn right. B comes from the left, going straight on. C is cycling straight on along the cycle track to your right, in your direction of travel. D is standing at the kerb of the road you are turning into, intending to cross it - and there is no pedestrian crossing marked there.

Four road users, three different provisions. In order:

C first. You are turning; C is going straight on alongside the carriageway in the same direction. § 9(3) sentence 1 StVO: "Anyone intending to turn must let oncoming vehicles through, and must also let rail vehicles, mopeds, bicycles and light electric vehicles through where they are travelling on or alongside the carriageway in the same direction."

D also goes before you - and this is the point of the picture. With no pedestrian crossing, § 25(3) sentence 1 StVO would require D to cross the carriageway "having regard to vehicular traffic"; on scenario 4's reasoning, D would be the one who has to wait. But because you are turning, § 9(3) sentence 3 StVO comes into play: "Particular consideration is to be shown to persons on foot; if necessary, one must wait." That duty does not depend on a marking - it depends on the fact that you are turning. This is exactly where the quick answer "no zebra crossing, so I go" falls apart.

And B? B has to wait - for you. § 8(1) sentence 1 StVO: "At crossroads and junctions, whoever comes from the right has priority." From B's point of view, you come from the right. The fact that you are turning changes nothing; § 8(2) sentence 4 StVO says so expressly: "Whoever has priority may not be substantially obstructed by the party required to wait, including while turning into the other road." So you keep your priority over B during the turn - and while you yourself are waiting for C and D.

Order: C and D, then A, then B.

Two traps in this picture. First: "someone is coming from the left, so they have priority" - right-before-left means whoever comes from the right has priority; a vehicle from the left is the one that must wait. Second: "I am turning, so I lose priority" - no; § 8(2) sentence 4 StVO says the opposite. What you have to defer on when turning is not your priority over B, but precedence over C and D - and that follows from § 9, not from § 8.

One assumption is built into this picture, deliberately: there are no signs 205, 206, 301 or 306, no traffic lights, no police officer, and neither road is a field or forest track. If any of those signs were present, the priority question between A and B would be answered differently under § 8(1) sentence 2 no. 1 StVO - the § 9(3) duties towards C and D would be unaffected.
fs-l2-s3.alt_text: Schematic top-down view of an unsigned crossroads. Vehicle A - blue, with a white roof dot, your car - approaches from the bottom; a curved arrow shows its right-turn path. Vehicle B - dark grey - approaches from the left; an arrow points straight ahead, to the right, into the junction. A red-brown cycle track runs across the junction to A's right; on it, C - a bicycle pictogram - goes straight on with an arrow pointing up, in the same direction as A. Further right, D - a pedestrian pictogram - stands at the lower kerb of the right-hand road; an arrow points across that road, upwards. No marking is drawn there.
fs-l2-s3.caption: Four road users, three provisions: § 9(3) sentence 1 (C), § 9(3) sentence 3 (D), § 8(1) sentence 1 and (2) sentence 4 (B).

fs-l2-s4.title: Five statements that hold - and four that do not
fs-l2-s4.body:
Five statements that carry most junction situations:

1. Right-before-left applies unless signs 205, 206, 301 or 306 order otherwise and nobody is coming from a field or forest track (§ 8(1) StVO). Light signals take precedence (§ 37(1) sentence 1 StVO), and a police officer's signals and instructions take precedence over all other rules (§ 36(1) StVO).
2. A bicycle on the carriageway is vehicle traffic like any other (§ 2(1) sentence 1 StVO). Right-before-left applies to the cyclist in the same way.
3. Turning is a separate set of duties. Anyone turning lets oncoming vehicles through, and bicycles travelling in the same direction on or alongside the carriageway (§ 9(3) sentence 1), and shows particular consideration to persons on foot, waiting where necessary (§ 9(3) sentence 3).
4. Pedestrian priority under § 26 StVO exists only at a pedestrian crossing. Elsewhere § 25(3) StVO applies: the carriageway is to be crossed having regard to vehicular traffic.
5. Whoever has priority keeps it while turning into the other road (§ 8(2) sentence 4 StVO).

Four statements that are often repeated and are not correct:

"Pedestrians always have priority." No. § 26(1) StVO applies at a pedestrian crossing, § 25(3) StVO elsewhere - and § 9(3) sentence 3 StVO applies on top when a vehicle is turning.

"Cyclists have to let cars go first." No. § 8(1) sentence 2 StVO recognises exactly two exceptions to right-before-left, and neither concerns bicycles.

"A cyclist has priority on a zebra crossing too." Not while riding. § 26(1) sentence 1 StVO names persons on foot and users of invalid carriages or wheelchairs. Dismounted and pushing: yes.

"If you have priority, you may drive." Only as far as § 1(2) StVO allows - nobody may be harmed or endangered. Being in the right and still braking is the normal case, not the exception.

Exam tip: in any task, first check whether anyone is turning and whether a marking is present. Those two facts decide the correct answer more often than the question of who comes from the right.

fs-l3.title: Video questions in the real theory exam

fs-l3-s1.title: Video questions: moving images in the theory exam since 2014
fs-l3-s1.body:
In the real theoretical driving-licence examination, not every task is a still image. Since 1 April 2014 the examination has also included tasks built around short film sequences, usually called Videofragen: you watch an animated clip of a traffic situation a few seconds long, from the driver's point of view, and are then asked about it on a still frame. The clip can be replayed several times before you answer; the answer itself is multiple choice, as in any other task.

Legally the format rests on § 16(2) sentence 1 FeV: "The examination is conducted by means of questions which may be posed in different forms and with the help of different media." Sentence 2 refers, for the examination's subject matter, form, scope, composition, conduct and assessment, to Annex 7 Part 1 FeV.

The details - how many such tasks appear in one examination, and how often a clip may be replayed - are not in the FeV itself but in the examination directive for the theoretical test and its question catalogue, published through the Verkehrsblatt (Verkehrsblatt document O 3210, which replaced the earlier documents S 3213 and B 3219 on 1 January 2021). In practice, two such video tasks are regularly set and the clip can be viewed up to five times. What governs is always the current version of the examination directive, not this summary - if in doubt, ask your driving school or the responsible technical testing centre.

Why the format exists: a still image can only test hazard perception up to a point. Whether a situation becomes dangerous depends on movement - on who is accelerating, who is easing into a gap, which area is currently obscured. § 16(1) no. 2 FeV requires the candidate to show that they are "familiar with the hazards of road traffic and with the conduct required to avert them". That is easier to test in a moving scene than in a photograph.

This course does not yet contain video clips of its own. The scenarios in the previous lessons are deliberately static diagrams: they test knowledge of the rules, not perception over time. Self-produced clips are planned and will be added here once they exist; this course will not contain reconstructions of actual examination videos.

fs-l3-s2.title: How to work through a moving-image task
fs-l3-s2.body:
An approach that fits video tasks as well as the static scenarios in this course:

First pass - orientation only. What kind of road is this, inside or outside a built-up area? Are there signs, markings, traffic lights? Who is actually in the picture? Do not look for the answer yet.

Second pass - read the movement. Who is speeding up, who is slowing down? Where is a gap opening that someone could turn into? Which area is currently obscured - between parked cars, behind a bus, behind a hedge? Obscured areas are the most common place where a hazard is first merely foreseeable and then suddenly present.

Third pass - work through the duties, in the order from the first lesson: special rule in force, is anyone turning, is a bicycle involved, is anyone on foot.

Then answer - keeping the basic rule in mind. § 1(1) StVO requires "constant caution and mutual consideration"; § 1(2) requires that "no other person is harmed, endangered, or obstructed or inconvenienced more than is unavoidable in the circumstances". In hazard-awareness tasks the correct answer is therefore almost always the more cautious one: come off the speed, increase the gap, be ready to brake - not "I have priority".

This lesson is background on the examination format and is not quizzed.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_verbot-s1.body:
You are driving on a fast road and see this traffic sign. What must you observe?

Correct answer: Turning around (U-turn) is prohibited on this stretch of road.

Sign 272 prohibits U-turns. On fast roads a U-turn manoeuvre is especially dangerous, which is why this prohibition is strictly imposed and enforced there.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_verbot-s2.body:
You are driving a truck and see this traffic sign showing 70m. What must you observe?

Correct answer: You must keep a minimum following distance of 70m to the vehicle ahead.

Sign 273 requires motor vehicles over 3.5t to keep a minimum following distance to the vehicle ahead, to avoid rear-end collisions if it brakes suddenly.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_verbot-s3.body:
A white round sign with a red border and a black number (e.g. '50') indicates:

Correct answer: Maximum permitted speed in km/h

Zeichen 274 sets the maximum permitted speed, which must not be exceeded.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_verbot-s4.body:
The same sign as the speed limit but crossed out in grey (Zeichen 278) means:

Correct answer: End of the previously ordered speed limit

A crossed-out sign cancels the previously applicable order.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_gefahr-s1.body:
A triangular warning sign showing playing children (Zeichen 136) warns of:

Correct answer: That children might suddenly run onto the road

The sign warns of children near the road, e.g. near schools or playgrounds; increased caution and readiness to brake are required.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_gefahr-s2.body:
A triangular warning sign with a train symbol (e.g. Zeichen 151) announces:

Correct answer: A level crossing without full or half barriers

Such signs announce level crossings without barriers, where special caution is required.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_gefahr-s3.body:
A triangular warning sign with a black saltire on a yellow background (sign 102) warns of:

Correct answer: A crossroads or junction where priority-to-the-right applies

This sign warns of an upcoming crossroads or junction with no priority signs, so the priority-to-the-right rule applies.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_gefahr-s4.body:
What does this sign warn of?

Correct answer: A risk of skidding or slipping, for example due to wetness or leaves.

Sign 114 warns of a risk of skidding or slipping. Adjust your speed and driving style to the road surface.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_sonstige-s.body:
A white sign with a red St. Andrew's cross (Zeichen 201) at a single-track level crossing means:

Correct answer: You must always stop if a rail vehicle is approaching

The St. Andrew's cross marks a level crossing; you must stop if a train is approaching.

What does this sign with three red stripes mean?

Correct answer: A railway crossing follows in about 240 metres.

Sign 156 is a three-stripe marker post before a railway crossing without barriers. The number of stripes decreases with distance: three stripes at about 240 m, two at 160 m, one at 80 m.

You enter a road marked with sign 330.1 (Autobahn). Which of the following statements are correct?

Correct answer: Pedestrians, cyclists and mopeds may not use the road / U-turns and reversing are prohibited / Only vehicles capable of at least 60 km/h may enter

On motorways (sign 330.1), pedestrians, cyclists and mopeds are banned, there is an effective minimum speed of around 60 km/h, and U-turns and reversing are prohibited. Stopping and parking are generally forbidden, except in emergencies or at designated areas.

What is this blue, pointed direction sign?

Correct answer: A direction sign pointing toward the motorway (Autobahn).

Sign 430, with a blue background and white lettering, shows the way to the motorway.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_gebot-s1.body:
A round blue sign with a white bicycle symbol (Zeichen 237) means:

Correct answer: Cycle path with mandatory use for cyclists

If a cycle path is marked with Zeichen 237, cyclists must use it, provided it is safe to use.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_gebot-s2.body:
A round blue sign with a pedestrian symbol above a bicycle symbol (Zeichen 240) means:

Correct answer: Shared pedestrian and cycle path

On a shared pedestrian and cycle path, pedestrians and cyclists must share the space and show mutual consideration.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_gebot-s3.body:
A round blue sign with a white arrow pointing right (Zeichen 209) means:

Correct answer: Mandatory direction of travel to the right

Mandatory direction arrows (Zeichen 209 ff.) require driving in the indicated direction.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_gebot-s4.body:
A blue round sign with three white arrows arranged in a circle (sign 215) means:

Correct answer: A roundabout, driving direction around the circle is mandatory

Sign 215 marks a roundabout and requires drivers to travel around it in the direction shown by the arrows.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_richt-s1.body:
What does this traffic sign mean?

Correct answer: A hikers' parking area for leaving your vehicle before a hike.

Sign 317 marks a hikers' parking area, where vehicles can be left before setting off on a hike.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_richt-s2.body:
What applies from this traffic sign onward?

Correct answer: The start of a traffic-calmed area; walking pace only, pedestrians may use the whole width.

Sign 325.1 marks the start of a traffic-calmed area, where walking pace applies and pedestrians may use the entire width of the area.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_richt-s3.body:
What does this traffic sign mean?

Correct answer: The end of a traffic-calmed area.

Sign 325.2 marks the end of a traffic-calmed area; ordinary traffic rules apply again from this point.

fuehrerschein-derived-zeichen_richt-s4.body:
What does this traffic sign indicate?

Correct answer: The start of a tunnel.

Sign 327 marks the start of a tunnel.

fuehrerschein-derived-gefahr-s1.body:
You are driving on the motorway in the rain. How does the braking distance change compared to a dry road?

Correct answer: It becomes clearly longer because the tyres grip less

A wet road reduces friction between tyre and surface. The car needs more distance to stop, so you must increase your following distance.

fuehrerschein-derived-gefahr-s2.body:
You are driving at 80 km/h. Roughly how long is your reaction distance before you even start braking?

Correct answer: About 24 metres

A simple rule of thumb: divide the speed in km/h by 10, then multiply by 3, to get the reaction distance in metres. At 80 km/h that is roughly 24 metres.

fuehrerschein-derived-gefahr-s3.body:
You see a ball roll onto the road from the roadside. How should you react?

Correct answer: Slow down at once and expect a child to run after the ball

A rolling ball is a classic warning sign that a child may run onto the road right after it without looking. Slowing down carefully and being ready to brake is important here.

fuehrerschein-derived-gefahr-s4.body:
A bus stops at a bus stop and signals with its indicator. What must you do as the driver of another vehicle?

Correct answer: Adjust your speed so the bus can pull out again if needed

When a bus at a stop signals, you must let it pull back into traffic and, if necessary, reduce your own speed.

fuehrerschein-derived-umwelt-s1.body:
Which driving style saves the most fuel?

Correct answer: Driving with foresight and shifting to a higher gear early

Anticipating traffic and avoiding heavy braking and acceleration clearly reduces fuel use. Shifting up early keeps the engine speed low and saves even more.

fuehrerschein-derived-umwelt-s2.body:
What is the minimum legal tread depth for a car tyre?

Correct answer: 1.6 millimetres

The legal minimum tread depth is 1.6 millimetres. For good safety in wet conditions, a much higher value is often recommended.

fuehrerschein-derived-umwelt-s3.body:
What effect does too-low tyre pressure have on fuel use and safety?

Correct answer: Fuel use rises and braking distance can get longer

Tyre pressure that is too low increases rolling resistance, which raises fuel use, and also worsens handling. Checking tyre pressure regularly is therefore worthwhile.

fuehrerschein-derived-umwelt-s4.body:
What does an ABS (anti-lock braking system) do?

Correct answer: It stops the wheels locking under hard braking, so you stay able to steer

ABS prevents the wheels from locking under hard braking. This keeps the vehicle steerable, even though the braking distance itself is not necessarily shortened by it.

fuehrerschein-derived-verhalten-s1.body:
You are the first to arrive at a road accident with injured people. What must you do first?

Correct answer: Secure the accident scene, then give first aid and call the emergency services

Anyone arriving at an accident must secure the scene, give first aid within their abilities, and alert the emergency services. Failing to help is a criminal offence.

fuehrerschein-derived-verhalten-s2.body:
You approach a railway crossing without barriers or flashing lights, but you see a train coming. What must you do?

Correct answer: Stop immediately, even though no warning signal is active

A visibly approaching train requires you to stop, regardless of whether a technical warning system has already been triggered.

fuehrerschein-derived-verhalten-s3.body:
On a two-lane motorway a traffic jam forms and an emergency vehicle needs to pass. How do you form an emergency corridor?

Correct answer: The left lane moves as far left as possible, all other lanes move as far right as possible

In slow-moving or stationary traffic on motorways and multi-lane roads, the leftmost lane must move left and all other lanes must move right, creating a corridor in the middle.

fuehrerschein-derived-verhalten-s4.body:
A school bus stops with its hazard lights on and children are getting off. How do you behave as a driver approaching or following?

Correct answer: Pass only at walking pace and be ready to stop if needed

When passing a stopped school bus with hazard lights on, you must drive at walking pace, because children may suddenly and carelessly step onto the road.

fuehrerschein-derived-autobahn-s1.body:
You have missed your exit on the motorway. What must you do?

Correct answer: Keep driving to the next exit

Turning around and reversing are forbidden on the motorway. A missed exit can only be corrected at the next exit.

fuehrerschein-derived-autobahn-s2.body:
Traffic on the motorway suddenly slows right down. When must you form an emergency lane?

Correct answer: As soon as traffic slows to walking pace or comes to a stop

An emergency lane must be formed immediately once traffic slows to walking pace or stops, not only once an emergency vehicle appears.

fuehrerschein-derived-autobahn-s3.body:
You are approaching a crest with poor visibility on a country road. May you overtake?

Correct answer: No, because you cannot see oncoming traffic in time

Overtaking is forbidden before crests and bends with poor visibility, because oncoming traffic would be spotted too late. This is one of the most dangerous causes of head-on collisions.

fuehrerschein-derived-autobahn-s4.body:
You overtake a cyclist outside built-up areas. What minimum lateral distance should you keep?

Correct answer: At least about 2 metres

When overtaking cyclists, a lateral distance of at least about 1.5 metres inside and about 2 metres outside built-up areas must be kept.

fuehrerschein-derived-parken-s1.body:
You want to get out of your parked car. What must you do beforehand?

Correct answer: Look back over your shoulder and make sure no cyclist or vehicle is approaching

Before getting out, you must make sure no cyclist or vehicle is passing. A carelessly opened door can seriously injure cyclists.

fuehrerschein-derived-parken-s2.body:
May you park near a level crossing?

Correct answer: No, parking is forbidden in the area before and after a level crossing

Parking before and after level crossings is forbidden, because visibility and free access for vehicles and barriers must be kept clear at all costs.

fuehrerschein-derived-parken-s3.body:
May you park in front of a fire station entrance or an area marked as a fire lane?

Correct answer: No, these access routes must remain clear at all times

Fire lanes and access routes to fire stations must remain clear at all times, so emergency vehicles can leave without delay.

fuehrerschein-derived-parken-s4.body:
What is the difference between 'stopping' (Halten) and 'parking' (Parken)?

Correct answer: It counts as parking if you stand still for more than three minutes or leave the vehicle

Standing still for more than three minutes or leaving the vehicle counts legally as parking. Briefer stops, for example to let someone in or out, count as stopping.

fuehrerschein-derived-ladung-s1.body:
Which combination of aids most effectively secures cargo in the boot against shifting?

Correct answer: An anti-slip mat combined with lashing straps

Anti-slip mats increase friction (force-locking), while lashing straps additionally prevent shifting (form-locking) – combining both is most effective.

fuehrerschein-derived-ladung-s2.body:
What must be considered regarding axle load when loading a vehicle?

Correct answer: The permitted axle load must not be exceeded on any axle and the vehicle must be loaded in a balanced way

Even if the total permitted weight is respected, no single axle may be overloaded, as this endangers steering and braking behaviour.

fuehrerschein-derived-ladung-s3.body:
What happens if a heavy, unsecured load slides forward during emergency braking?

Correct answer: It can dangerously strike occupants and affect the vehicle's braking behaviour

A shifting load acts like a projectile and can seriously injure occupants and unpredictably change the vehicle's handling.

fuehrerschein-derived-ladung-s4.body:
What determines the maximum permitted load for a roof rack or roof box?

Correct answer: The manufacturer's specified roof load and the vehicle's permitted axle load/total mass

Both the vehicle manufacturer and the roof rack manufacturer specify maximum roof loads, which must be respected together with the vehicle's permitted total mass.

fuehrerschein-derived-erstehilfe-s1.body:
You are involved in a traffic accident. What duties do you have under §34 StVO?

Correct answer: Stop immediately and secure the accident scene / Provide your name, address and driving licence on request / Give first aid to injured persons

Those involved in an accident must stop immediately, secure the scene, give first aid to the injured, and identify themselves on request. Leaving before identities are established, without a reasonable waiting period, constitutes unlawfully leaving the scene of an accident - so immediate departure is incorrect.

fuehrerschein-derived-erstehilfe-s2.body:
You are the first to arrive at a fresh accident scene. What should you do first?

Correct answer: Secure the scene (hazard lights, warning vest, warning triangle)

Before helping, the scene must be secured so no further people get injured.

fuehrerschein-derived-erstehilfe-s3.body:
At roughly what distance should you place the warning triangle before an accident on a rural road?

Correct answer: About 100 meters

On rural roads a rough guideline of about 100 meters gives following traffic enough time to react.

fuehrerschein-derived-erstehilfe-s4.body:
Before which type of stretch should the warning triangle be placed noticeably farther than the usual ~100 meters?

Correct answer: A blind curve or hillcrest

Before curves or hillcrests, drivers need more time to spot the danger, so the distance is increased (often 150-400 meters on motorways).

fuehrerschein-derived-fahrtuechtigkeit-s.body:
From which blood alcohol level does the 0.5 per mille limit apply as an administrative offence for experienced drivers?

Correct answer: From 0.5 per mille

From 0.5 per mille it is an administrative offence with a fine, points, and usually a driving ban.

From which blood alcohol level is a driver considered absolutely unfit to drive, treated as a criminal offence regardless of driving behaviour?

Correct answer: From 1.1 per mille

From 1.1 per mille a driver is considered absolutely unfit to drive; this is a criminal offence under §316 StGB, even without noticeably erratic driving.

What blood alcohol limit applies during the probationary period and for novice drivers under 21?

Correct answer: 0.0 per mille

For novice drivers in the probationary period and all drivers under 21, an absolute alcohol ban applies while driving.

What does the so-called 0.3 per mille threshold mean in German case law?

Correct answer: Already from 0.3 per mille it can be treated as a criminal offence if driving errors or an accident also occur

Under so-called relative unfitness to drive, alcohol-related driving errors or an accident from around 0.3 per mille onward can already lead to criminal liability.

fuehrerschein-derived-anhaenger_be-s1.body:
What check is mandatory before setting off after coupling a trailer?

Correct answer: It must be verified that the coupling has engaged securely and is mechanically locked (e.g. safety pin/lever engaged)

A coupling that has not fully engaged or is not secured can come loose while driving. The mechanical lock must therefore be checked (e.g. by lifting or pulling on it) before every trip.

fuehrerschein-derived-anhaenger_be-s2.body:
What is the function of the breakaway cable on a braked trailer?

Correct answer: If the trailer accidentally uncouples, it automatically activates the trailer's brake so it comes to a stop

If the trailer accidentally detaches from the towing vehicle, the breakaway cable pulls on the trailer's brake and applies it automatically, preventing it from rolling away uncontrolled. This is a key safety feature on braked trailers.

fuehrerschein-derived-anhaenger_be-s3.body:
Why should the trailer's indicators and brake lights be checked by a second person before setting off with a trailer?

Correct answer: Because a faulty electrical connector can mean other road users don't see the trailer's brake or turn signals, which is a significant accident risk

The electrical connector transmits signals for indicators, brake lights and general lighting from the towing vehicle to the trailer. A poor connection can cause these safety-relevant signals to fail without the driver noticing.

fuehrerschein-derived-anhaenger_be-s4.body:
What is trailer nose weight (Stützlast) and why is it safety-relevant?

Correct answer: It is the vertical force with which the trailer drawbar presses on the towing vehicle's coupling; it must stay within the limits rated by the manufacturer for both vehicle and coupling

Nose weight affects the towing vehicle's axle load and thus steering behaviour and braking. Too little nose weight promotes trailer sway, too much overloads the rear axle and coupling – both are dangerous and must stay within rated limits.
